title: Kohlhaas v. State
description: Whether Alaska's Initiative 2, which implemented an open nonpartisan primary and ranked-choice voting, violates political parties' associational rights, the constitutional provisions for electing the lieutenant governor, or the constitutional provisions for electing the governor.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that Initiative 2 infringed on political parties' associational rights by altering the primary system and allowing candidates to list party affiliation without endorsement, violated the constitutional method for nominating the lieutenant governor by pairing candidates, and unconstitutionally burdened the right to vote by adopting ranked-choice voting which they claimed required a majority or denied victory to the first-round plurality winner.
defendant_argument: The defendants contended that Initiative 2 did not burden associational rights as it decoupled state elections from party nominations and included disclaimers, that it complied with the constitutional provisions for the lieutenant governor by allowing joint tickets and flexible nomination methods, and that ranked-choice voting was a single tabulation process that did not require a majority to win and served important regulatory interests without unconstitutionally burdening the right to vote.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the superior court's judgment, ruling that Initiative 2 is constitutional and does not violate the Alaska Constitution.

title: State Department of Education & Early Development v. Alexander
description: Whether Alaska statutes permitting public funds for correspondence study programs, which can be used for private school tuition, violate the state constitution's prohibition against direct benefits to religious or other private educational institutions.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff (Alexander) argued that the statutes allowing public funds for correspondence study, particularly for private school tuition, are facially unconstitutional or unconstitutional as applied, violating the state constitution's prohibition against direct benefits to private educational institutions.
defendant_argument: The defendant (State Department of Education) argued that the statutes are facially constitutional because they have a "plainly legitimate sweep" with many valid uses of funds, even if some applications (like private school tuition) might be unconstitutional. Intervenor-appellants (Moceri) argued that the benefit to private schools is indirect and thus permissible.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the superior court's judgment, ruling that the allotment and ILP statutes are not facially unconstitutional and remanding the case for further proceedings, declining to rule on the constitutionality of using funds for private school tuition at this stage.

title: Valoaga v. State
description: Whether the Alaska Constitution requires a clear and convincing evidence standard for prison disciplinary proceedings, as argued by the plaintiff, or if a preponderance of the evidence standard is constitutionally permissible, as argued by the defendant.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the Alaska Constitution requires a clear and convincing evidence standard for prison disciplinary proceedings for major infractions, and that the DOC's failure to offer a saliva test violated his due process rights.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the preponderance of the evidence standard is constitutionally permissible in prison disciplinary proceedings and that the plaintiff's argument regarding saliva tests was not preserved for review.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the superior court's decision, ruling that the Alaska Constitution permits the use of a preponderance of the evidence standard in prison disciplinary proceedings and that the argument regarding saliva tests was waived.

title: Alaska Trappers Association v. City of Valdez
description: Whether a city ordinance limiting trapping in certain areas is preempted by state law or unconstitutional due to the state's pervasive authority over natural resources.
plaintiff_argument: The Alaska Trappers Association argued that the city's trapping ordinance is preempted by state law, violates AS 16.05.790 and article VIII of the Alaska Constitution, and that the state has exclusive jurisdiction over natural resource management, making the ordinance an improper veto of state determinations.
defendant_argument: The City of Valdez argued it has constitutional and statutory authority to regulate land use and public safety, and its ordinance is a valid exercise of municipal authority that is not expressly or impliedly prohibited by state law, with only an incidental effect on wildlife management.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the superior court's grant of summary judgment to the City of Valdez, upholding the city's ordinance.

title: State v. McKelvey
description: Whether police must obtain a warrant before using an airplane with a zoom lens to photograph a person's yard, or if such aerial surveillance falls under the 'open view' doctrine due to common small airplane travel in Alaska.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that because small airplane travel is common in Alaska and any passenger might peer into a yard, law enforcement officials should be allowed to do the same without a warrant, and that the 'open view' doctrine applies to aerial observations.
defendant_argument: McKelvey argued that the warrantless observation of his home with a telephoto lens during a flight constituted an illegal search, violating his reasonable expectation of privacy under the Alaska Constitution.
decision_outcome: The Alaska Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, holding that law enforcement officials must obtain a warrant before using aircraft and vision-enhancing technology to observe the curtilage of a person's home that is protected from ground-level observation.

title: Vazquez v. State
description: Whether Jennie Armstrong met the constitutional three-year Alaska residency requirement to be eligible to serve in the legislature.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that Armstrong did not establish Alaska residency until June 7, 2019, at the earliest, making her ineligible for the 2022 election.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that Armstrong established Alaska residency on May 20, 2019, thereby meeting the three-year residency requirement for the 2022 election.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the superior court's conclusion that Jennie Armstrong is eligible to serve in the legislature, finding she established residency on May 20, 2019.

title: Native Village of Kwinhagak v. State, Department of Health & Social Services
description: Whether the Office of Children's Services (OCS) must follow civil commitment statutes when admitting a child in its custody to a hospital for psychiatric treatment, and whether a 46-day hospitalization without a prompt hearing violates the child's constitutional due process rights.
plaintiff_argument: The Native Village of Kwinhagak argued that OCS must follow civil commitment statutes for psychiatric hospitalization and that the prolonged hospitalization without a prompt hearing violated the child's constitutional due process rights.
defendant_argument: The State of Alaska argued that OCS has authority under CINA statutes to admit children to psychiatric care, not civil commitment statutes, and that existing injunctions provided sufficient procedural protections.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the superior court's order, ruling that OCS was not required to follow civil commitment statutes for psychiatric hospitalization but that the 46-day delay in holding a hearing violated the child's procedural due process rights.

title: Sitka Tribe of Alaska v. State
description: Whether the Alaska Department of Fish and Game has a constitutional duty to provide all relevant information to the Board of Fisheries for natural resource management decisions, and whether the Sitka Tribe of Alaska was entitled to a preliminary injunction and attorney's fees.
plaintiff_argument: The Tribe argued that the Alaska Constitution's sustained yield clause requires the Department to provide all relevant information to the Board, that it faced irreparable harm warranting a preliminary injunction, and that it was the prevailing party for attorney's fees.
defendant_argument: The State and Alliance argued there is no constitutional duty for the Department to provide all relevant information, that the Tribe did not demonstrate irreparable harm for an injunction, and that the superior court's denial of attorney's fees to all parties was not an abuse of discretion.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the superior court's decisions, denying the Tribe's constitutional claim, denying its request for a preliminary injunction, and denying attorney's fees to all parties.

title: Taylor v. Alaska Legislative Affairs Agency
description: Whether the Alaska Constitution bars a lawsuit that Alaska Attorney General Treg R. Taylor brought against the Legislative Affairs Agency, with the plaintiff arguing it is not barred and the defendant arguing it is.
plaintiff_argument: Attorney General Taylor argued his lawsuit was not constitutionally barred, asserting common law authority to sue on the State's behalf distinct from the governor's constitutional authority, and that prior precedent allowed challenges to non-legislative acts.
defendant_argument: The Legislative Affairs Agency argued that the lawsuit was barred by Article III, Section 16 of the Alaska Constitution as an action brought 'in the name of the State' and 'against the legislature,' contending that an attorney general's authority is substantively the same as a governor's.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the superior court's decision that Attorney General Taylor's lawsuit was unconstitutional and barred by Article III, Section 16 of the Alaska Constitution, but vacated and remanded the attorney's fees award for further proceedings.

title: Williams Alaska Petroleum, Inc. v. State
description: Whether Williams Alaska Petroleum, Inc. is strictly liable for sulfolane and PFAS contamination, associated damages, and remediation costs, and whether the superior court's decision violated Williams's due process rights or constituted an unconstitutional taking.
plaintiff_argument: The State and Flint Hills argued that Williams is strictly liable for sulfolane and PFAS releases, that sulfolane is a hazardous substance, and that Williams must pay damages, response costs, and contribute to remediation.
defendant_argument: Williams argued that sulfolane is not a hazardous substance, that the awarded damages and costs were erroneous, that the injunctive and declaratory relief was improper, that the purchase agreement was misinterpreted regarding liability allocation, and that the decision violated due process and constituted an unconstitutional taking.
decision_outcome: The court largely affirmed the superior court's decision, concluding that Williams is strictly liable for sulfolane and PFAS releases, awarding response costs and natural resource damages to the State and Flint Hills, and affirming contribution awards, but remanded the injunctive relief for more specificity.

title: In re Abigail B.
description: Whether the lengthy delays between individuals' pre-evaluation detentions and their transportation to an evaluation facility violated their substantive due process rights.
plaintiff_argument: Abigail and Jethro argued that their prolonged pre-evaluation detentions violated their substantive due process rights because the nature and duration of the detentions were not reasonably related to the purpose of facilitating immediate transportation for evaluation.
defendant_argument: The State argued that broader purposes for pre-evaluation detention, such as protecting vulnerable individuals and society, justified the detentions, and that the detentions were reasonably related to these broader purposes.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the superior court orders that authorized the continued pre-evaluation detention of Abigail and Jethro following their review hearings.

title: In re 2021 Redistricting Cases
description: Whether the Alaska Redistricting Board's final and amended redistricting plans for House and Senate districts comply with constitutional requirements regarding gerrymandering, socioeconomic integration, compactness, and public hearing procedures.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the Board's redistricting plans for various House and Senate districts were unconstitutional due to political gerrymandering, lack of socioeconomic integration, non-compactness, population deviations, due process violations, and failure to hold meaningful public hearings.
defendant_argument: The Board contended that its redistricting plans were constitutional, complied with all legal requirements, and did not involve unconstitutional gerrymandering or other violations, asserting that the superior court erred in its findings.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the unconstitutionality of Senate Districts K, E, and L due to political gerrymandering, reversed the superior court's finding on House Districts 3 and 4, and found the "Cantwell Appendage" in House District 36 unconstitutional for lack of compactness, while affirming the interim plan for 2022 elections and remanding for a final plan.

title: Knolmayer v. McCollum
description: Whether Alaska Statute 09.55.548(b), which limits the recovery of damages compensated by collateral sources, violates the equal protection guarantee of the Alaska Constitution when applied to a medical malpractice claimant whose insurer has a contractual right to reimbursement.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that AS 09.55.548(b) violates equal protection by creating an unfair distinction between different types of medical malpractice claimants, leading to a 'double deduction' and forcing them to bear the loss, which is contrary to legislative intent.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that AS 09.55.548(b) is a legislative policy choice to reduce damages awards and that its classifications are subject to minimum scrutiny, bearing a fair and substantial relation to the legitimate government objective of eliminating double recoveries.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the superior court's order and remanded the case, concluding that AS 09.55.548(b)'s limitation on recovery of collateral source compensation violates Alaska's equal protection clause when applied to a claimant who receives compensation from a collateral source that exercises a right of reimbursement against the claimant's recovery.

title: Short v. State
description: Whether the Higher Education Investment Fund (HEIF) is subject to the state's annual budgetary "sweep" provision, with the students arguing it is not sweepable due to prior appropriation and the Executive Branch arguing it is sweepable under constitutional provisions and precedent.
plaintiff_argument: The students argued that the HEIF is not sweepable because its appropriations do not lapse and the funds have already been validly appropriated and expended for investments. They also contended that making the HEIF sweepable would violate the separation of powers and that the controlling precedent, Cowper, was erroneous and should be overturned.
defendant_argument: The Executive Branch argued that the HEIF is sweepable under existing case law (Hickel v. Cowper) and the plain language of Article IX, Section 17 of the Alaska Constitution, because further legislative appropriations are required for its expenditure. They maintained that the sweep is a constitutional mandate and does not violate the separation of powers.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Alaska affirmed the superior court's decision, ruling that the Higher Education Investment Fund (HEIF) is sweepable under the state's constitutional provisions.

title: Department of Corrections v. Stefano
description: Whether the superior court has appellate jurisdiction to review the Department of Corrections' (DOC) decision to remove an inmate from electronic monitoring, and whether DOC's decision implicates the inmate's constitutional rights to due process and rehabilitation.
plaintiff_argument: Stefano argued that his removal from electronic monitoring violated his constitutional rights to due process and rehabilitation, and that the superior court had appellate jurisdiction to review DOC's decision because it involved fundamental constitutional rights and an adjudicative record.
defendant_argument: The Department of Corrections (DOC) argued that the superior court lacked appellate jurisdiction to review its decision, that electronic monitoring is not a formal rehabilitative program, and that its decision to remove Stefano did not implicate a fundamental constitutional right to rehabilitation or produce an adjudicative record for review.
decision_outcome: The court held that serving a sentence on electronic monitoring affords a limited but constitutionally protected degree of liberty, requiring due process for removal. However, the court also held that the superior court lacked appellate jurisdiction to review DOC's decision in this case because DOC's decisional process was not an adjudicative proceeding and did not create an adequate record for appellate review. The court vacated the superior court's decision and remanded the case to be converted into a civil action for judicial review.

title: State v. The Alaska Legislative Council
description: Whether forward funding for public education, which appropriates funds for future fiscal years, is consistent with the annual budgeting process established by the Alaska Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The Alaska Legislative Council and Coalition for Education Equity argued that forward-funded appropriations for public education were consistent with the legislature's constitutional authority and did not violate any specific constitutional provision, and that the governor's refusal to disburse funds violated his duty to faithfully execute the laws.
defendant_argument: The State of Alaska, Governor Mike Dunleavy, argued that forward funding violated the annual appropriations model established by the Alaska Constitution, infringing on the governor's veto power and the prohibition on dedicating revenues.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the superior court's decision, concluding that forward-funded appropriations are unconstitutional and vacated the attorney's fees awards.

title: State v. Graham
description: Whether the superior court erred in sentencing Stacey Graham for second-degree murder, specifically regarding the application of sentencing benchmarks, aggravating factors, the consideration of general deterrence and community condemnation, and the admissibility of victim impact evidence (police testimony and tribute videos).
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the superior court properly applied sentencing benchmarks and aggravating factors, did not give undue weight to deterrence and community condemnation, and that the judge's recusal was unnecessary despite evidentiary errors.
defendant_argument: Graham argued his sentence was excessive, contending the superior court erred in applying sentencing benchmarks, improperly relied on general deterrence and community condemnation, and abused its discretion by admitting prejudicial victim impact evidence, necessitating resentencing by a different judge.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision regarding sentencing standards and judge recusal, but affirmed that the superior court abused its discretion by admitting police officer testimony and victim tribute videos without proper review, vacating the sentence and remanding for resentencing by the same judge.

title: Association of Village Council Presidents Regional Housing Authority v. Mael
description: Whether the housing authority owed a tort duty to inspect the boiler with reasonable care, whether the boiler explosion was caused by a product defect or negligence, and whether the statutory noneconomic damages cap should be applied to Dietrich Mael's award and aggregated with his family members' awards.
plaintiff_argument: Dietrich Mael argued that the housing authority had an independent tort duty to inspect the boiler, that its negligence caused the explosion, and that the statutory damages cap violated his due process rights by not accounting for inflation or severe injuries, and that family members' NIED claims should not be aggregated under the same cap.
defendant_argument: The housing authority argued it had no tort duty to inspect the boiler, that the explosion was caused by a product defect, and that all noneconomic damages, including those for family members' negligent infliction of emotional distress, should be aggregated under a single statutory damages cap.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the superior court's judgment, upholding that the housing authority had a tort duty to inspect the boiler, that its negligence caused the explosion, that Dietrich's noneconomic damages were subject to a $1 million cap, and that his family members' emotional distress damages were subject to separate caps.

title: Dutchess v. Dutch
description: Whether the superior court erred in granting the father sole legal custody to make vaccination decisions for their minor children, despite the mother's religious objections and claims of constitutional violations.
plaintiff_argument: The mother argued that granting the father sole legal custody for vaccination decisions infringed upon her constitutional right to free exercise of religion and violated her due process rights.
defendant_argument: The father argued that vaccinating the children was in their best interests, as recommended by their pediatrician, and sought sole legal custody for vaccination decisions.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the superior court's order, granting the father sole legal authority to make vaccination decisions for the children.

title: Sagoonick v. State
description: Whether the State of Alaska's resource development policies, which contribute to climate change, violate the constitutional rights of young Alaskans to a stable climate system and the State's duty to protect natural resources.
plaintiff_argument: The young Alaskans argued that the State's resource development policies and actions contribute to climate change, violating their constitutional rights to a stable climate system and the State's public trust duty to protect natural resources, and sought to compel the State to adopt a climate recovery plan and reduce carbon emissions.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the plaintiffs' claims involved non-justiciable political questions, better left to the legislative and executive branches, and that the Department's denial of the rulemaking petition was consistent with statutory requirements and not arbitrary.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the superior court's dismissal of the lawsuit, ruling that the injunctive relief claims presented non-justiciable political questions and the declaratory relief claims were properly dismissed on prudential grounds, and that the Department's denial of the rulemaking petition was not arbitrary.

title: Department of Administration v. Retired Public Employees of Alaska, Inc.
description: Whether the State's 2014 revision of the dental insurance plan for public retirees unconstitutionally diminished accrued benefits, and whether the analysis of diminishment should include the premium rates paid by retirees.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the 2014 dental plan diminished retirees' accrued benefits and that the premiums paid by retirees are irrelevant to the diminishment analysis.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the dental plan was not an accrued benefit, or if it was, the court erred by not considering premium rates in the diminishment analysis.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the superior court's judgment and remanded the case for a new diminishment analysis that includes consideration of premium rates, while affirming that the option to purchase dental insurance is an accrued benefit.

title: Dunleavy v. Alaska Legislative Council ex rel. Alaska State Legislature
description: Whether legislative inaction on gubernatorial appointments, as defined by statute, is equivalent to a denial of confirmation, or if appointees remain in office until the legislature affirmatively votes on their confirmation.
plaintiff_argument: The Legislative Council argued that legislative inaction on gubernatorial appointments, as defined by statute, is tantamount to a denial of confirmation, meaning those appointees cannot continue to serve.
defendant_argument: The Governor argued that his appointees remain in office until the legislature affirmatively votes to confirm or reject them, and that laws defining inaction as rejection are unconstitutional.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the superior court's judgment, ruling that the statutes defining legislative inaction as a denial of confirmation violate the Alaska Constitution.

title: State v. Arctic Village Council
description: Whether the absentee ballot witness requirement unconstitutionally burdened the right to vote during the COVID-19 pandemic.
plaintiff_argument: The witness requirement forced voters, especially vulnerable ones, to risk their health to vote or forgo voting, thus unconstitutionally burdening their fundamental right to vote during the pandemic.
defendant_argument: The witness requirement was necessary to deter fraud and promote voter confidence, and the plaintiffs unreasonably delayed in bringing the suit, making their claims barred by laches.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the superior court's decision to grant a preliminary injunction, suspending the absentee ballot witness requirement for the 2020 general election.

title: State v. Recall Dunleavy
description: Whether the recall application against Governor Dunleavy satisfied the legal requirements for presentation to the voters, with the recall committee arguing for its sufficiency and the State arguing against it.
plaintiff_argument: The recall committee (Recall Dunleavy) argued that their application, citing lack of fitness, incompetence, and neglect of duties, was legally and factually sufficient to proceed to a recall election.
defendant_argument: The State of Alaska argued that the recall application was not legally or factually sufficient to meet the statutory grounds for recall.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the superior court's decision, ruling that the recall committee's application satisfied the legal requirements for presentation to the voters.

title: State v. Galvin
description: Whether the Division of Elections' ballot design, which omitted Alyse Galvin's nonpartisan voter registration, violated a statutory directive to designate a candidate's party affiliation on the ballot and Galvin's right to free political association under the Alaska Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The Division's ballot design, by omitting her nonpartisan voter registration, violated a statutory directive and her right to free political association under the Alaska Constitution.
defendant_argument: Granting an injunction to change the ballot design would jeopardize the prospects of a successful and timely election, imperiling the public interest, and the terms 'party affiliation' and 'party designation' were synonymous.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the superior court's denial of Alyse Galvin's request for a preliminary injunction, concluding that granting the injunction would have imperiled the public interest in an orderly and timely election.

title: Watson v. State
description: Whether the Alaska statute that excludes misdemeanor traffic violations from juvenile court jurisdiction violates a minor's right to equal protection under the Alaska Constitution, with the plaintiff arguing it creates unfair differential treatment and the defendant arguing it is a reasonable measure for public safety and juvenile rehabilitation.
plaintiff_argument: Elizabeth Watson argued that the statute violates her equal protection rights because it unfairly treats minors accused of misdemeanor DUI differently from those accused of other misdemeanors in juvenile court and from those accused of felony DUI who are charged in juvenile court.
defendant_argument: The State of Alaska argued that the statute is constitutional because the legislature can reasonably treat driving offenses uniformly for public safety and deter bad driving, while also protecting juvenile offenders from the harsh consequences of felony convictions.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's judgment, concluding that the statute requiring minors accused of non-felony traffic offenses to be charged as adults is constitutional and does not violate equal protection.

title: Metcalfe v. State
description: Whether the repeal of a statutory provision allowing former state employees to reinstate their credited service and original benefits tier upon re-employment and repayment of withdrawn contributions diminished or impaired an accrued benefit of the retirement system, protected by Article XII, Section 7 of the Alaska Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the statutory right to reinstate credited service was an accrued benefit protected by Article XII, Section 7 of the Alaska Constitution, and its repeal unconstitutionally diminished that benefit.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the reinstatement right was not an accrued benefit protected by the constitution, as it was an employment benefit, not a membership benefit, and only applied to active members, not former members, and was merely an offer that could be revoked.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the superior court's summary judgment order, ruling that the statutory reinstatement right was an accrued benefit protected by the constitution and its repeal was unconstitutional.
